title: File:Ingenuity flight 4 animation (vertical).gif
description:
NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter took these images on its fourth flight, on April 30, 2021, using its navigation camera. The camera, which tracks surface features below the helicopter, takes images at a rate at which the helicopter’s blades appear frozen in place, despite making 21 full rotations in-between each image. In flight, the blades spin at 2,537 rpm. The images are aligned entirely using Ingenuity's on-board position tracking system highlighting the stability and accuracy of the navigation algorithm.
The Ingenuity Mars Helicopter was built by JPL, which also manages the technology demonstration project for NASA Headquarters. It is supported by NASA’s Science, Aeronautics Research, and Space Technology mission directorates. NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley, and NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, provided significant flight performance analysis and technical assistance during Ingenuity’s development. AeroVironment Inc., Qualcomm, and SolAero also provided design assistance and major vehicle components. Lockheed Martin Space designed and manufactured the Mars Helicopter Delivery System.

title: File:Ingenuity flight 25 full real-time animation.gif
description:
This is the real-time animation where each frame displayed at 1 fps rate. For this animation of flight 25 of Ingenuity 190 frames acquired by the navigation camera (NAV) of the helicopter were used.

Animation starts from the photo taken at 10:02:57 local mean solar time on April 8, 2022 (sol 403 of the Perseverance rover mission), when its 1 metre (3.3 ft) above martian surface after departure. Timestamp for the last photo is 11:05:31, when Ingenuity has almost 1 metre (3.3 ft) above the martian surface before landing at Airfield Q 161.3 seconds of flight.

The navigation camera has been programmed to deactivate whenever the rotorcraft is within 1 m (3.3 ft) of the surface. This helps ensure any dust kicked up during takeoff and landing won’t interfere with the navigation system as it tracks features on the ground.

Images credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

title: File:Lufthansa Flight 2904.gif
description: Lufthansa Flight 2904's brakes did not engage until both main gear struts were in contact with the ground. The pilot's standard operating procedure for a windsheer landing was to increase speed and put the right main gear on the runway first.

title: File:Animated gif - the flight James Webb Space Telescope Telescope Structure (21225094706).gif
artist: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope from Greenbelt, MD, USA
description:
The James Webb Space Telescope's flight telescope structure was recently moved from its shipping container by crane in the big cleanroom NASA Goddard. The telescope structure is like the "bones" of the observatory - it will support the mirrors and instruments, all of which will be installed here at Goddard over the next year or so.

title: File:Perseverance's Navcam View of Ingenuity's First Flight (PIA24586).gif
description:
NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter achieves powered, controlled flight for the first time on another planet, hovering for several seconds before touching back down on April 19, 2021. The image was taken by the Navigation Camera, or Navcam, aboard the agency’s Perseverance Mars rover from a distance of 210 feet (64 meters).

The Ingenuity Mars Helicopter was built by JPL, which also manages this technology demonstration project for NASA Headquarters. It is supported by NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, Aeronautics Research Mission Directorate, and Space Technology Mission Directorate. NASA’s Ames Research Center and Langley Research Center provided significant flight performance analysis and technical assistance during Ingenuity’s development.

A key objective for Perseverance’s mission on Mars is astrobiology, including the search for signs of ancient microbial life. The rover will characterize the planet’s geology and past climate, pave the way for human exploration of the Red Planet, and be the first mission to collect and cache Martian rock and regolith (broken rock and dust).

Subsequent NASA missions, in cooperation with ESA (European Space Agency), would send spacecraft to Mars to collect these sealed samples from the surface and return them to Earth for in-depth analysis.

The Mars 2020 Perseverance mission is part of NASA’s Moon to Mars exploration approach, which includes Artemis missions to the Moon that will help prepare for human exploration of the Red Planet.

JPL, which is managed for NASA by Caltech in Pasadena, California, built and manages operations of the Perseverance rover.

title: File:Ingenuity pre-flight 14 blade speed rotation test on sol 204.gif
description:
Preliminary speed blade rotation test on sol 204 conducted on the eve of flight #14.

This animation is compiled from two images that NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter acquired these images using its navigation camera:

  • https://mars.nasa.gov/mars2020-raw-images/pub/ods/surface/sol/00204/ids/edr/browse/heli/HNM_0204_0685045539_651ECM_N0130001HELI00052_0000LUJ01.png

on September 16, 2021 (sol 204 of the Perseverance rover mission) at the local mean solar time of 11:11:00 and 11:12:59 respectively

This camera is mounted in the helicopter’s fuselage and pointed directly downward to track the ground during flight.
